sources.title: Shirase Nobu (Q715832), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-13): English label 'Nobu Shirase', description 'Japanese explorer of the Antarctic (1861-1946)', Japanese label 白瀬矗, Korean label 시라세 노부, born 1861-07-20, died 1946-09-04, instance of human, citizen of Japan. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

English Wikipedia, 'Nobu Shirase' (read for orientation and to locate the independent sources below; its infobox birth date of 13 June 1861 is the same date as the Japanese lunar-calendar date the National Diet Library converts to 20 July 1861). Not used as support for any row or card.

Susan Barr (Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage), 'The Japanese Antarctic Expedition in 1912: a summary of lectures given at the Norway-Japan Society and the Mariners Society in Oslo, 2012', Nankyoku Shiryo (Antarctic Record) vol. 57 no. 2, 2013, pp. 299-307 (National Institute of Polar Research; read in full from the archived PDF). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: a polar historian's account based mainly on the translated 1913 expedition report and the Shirase Memorial Museum paper, with the diaries of the Fram's crew as an outside voice. It covers the ambition from boyhood, the 1893-95 Kuril expedition (ten of the party died in the first winter and three of five newcomers in the second, and he stayed the second year), the 1909 switch from the North to the South Pole, the Diet's vote of funds that the government refused to pay and the private supporters' association, the 204-ton converted fisheries ship, the late departure on 29 November 1910, the failed first season (74 degrees 16 minutes S), the wintering at Sydney with Edgeworth David's help, the change of aim from the Pole to exploration in two parties, the meeting with the Fram in the Bay of Whales on 16-17 January 1912, the Dash Patrol to 80 degrees 05 minutes S on 28 January, the return to Tokyo on 20 June 1912 with all men in good health, the debts that took until 1935 to clear, and the later naming of the Shirase icebreakers. Contains the Fram officers' unflattering notes on the Japanese handling of seals. A report of two lectures rather than an academic study, as its editors say.

Stephanie Pain, 'Scott, Amundsen... and Nobu Shirase', New Scientist, 24-31 December 2011 (read in full from a complete reproduction of the feature on a blog mirror, not at newscientist.com): a science-journalism account that draws on the New Zealand and Australian press of 1911 and on the historians Ben McInnes and William Stevenson. It reports his regimen of no drink, tobacco, fire or hot food, his January 1910 appeal to the Diet, the public and press indifference, Okuma's rescue of the funding, the ill-prepared look of the ship and the 'toy' sledges, the retreat to Sydney and the local suspicion, the decision to settle for science and then still make a southward dash, the halt at 80 degrees 5 minutes S, the heavy debts, and the historians' verdict that the scientific results were minimal and that the expedition was heroic. Uses Shirase's 1913 account for the dash itself.

Rupert Summerson, 'Nankyoku no kyoku: The cultural life of the Shirase Antarctic Expedition 1910-12', in the ANU Press volume 'Antarctica: Music, Sounds and Cultural Connections' (2015; chapter read in full). An independent academic chapter that surveys the English and Japanese literature (Hamre 1933, the 2011 translation of the expedition report, the Australian theses of McInnes and Stevenson, Chet Ross's bibliography) and gives a dated route of both voyages: Tokyo 1 December 1910, Wellington, Sydney on 1 May 1911 where the party wintered at Parsley Bay, secretary Tada and Captain Nomura sent home for funds and dogs, departure on 19 November 1911, the Dash Patrol of five from 20 to 31 January 1912, the 14 February conference that judged the aims achieved, and the return on 20 June 1912. Also records that Shirase's secretary Tada fell out with him and was demoted. Concludes that despite the lack of official support Shirase's determination made Japan a member of the club of Antarctic nations.

Australian Museum, 'Japanese Antarctica expedition and the Shirase sword' and the Museum blog post 'Our Global Neighbours: Nobu Shirase' by Stan Florek (both read in full). A museum history with dated quotations from the Sydney press of 1911: Professor Edgeworth David's public defence of the expedition against the suspicion that the Japanese were spies, his praise at a Town Hall lecture in June 1911, his practical help with equipping the ship, Shirase's farewell gift to him of a samurai sword on 19 November 1911, and Shirase's own remark that it was fortunate David lived in Sydney. The blog adds that Shirase's funding came partly from small donations by students, and that he spent his last years in a rented room above a fish shop. The blog's statement that Shirase spent 1893-94 in the Alaskan Arctic conflicts with the Kuril account in the other sources and is not used.

Dictionary of Sydney (archived 2021), 'Japanese Antarctic expedition camp at Parsley Bay 1911' (read in full): the Kainan Maru at Parsley Bay and then Double Bay and Balmain for repairs, the White Australia Act exemption that let the scientists land, the Wentworth estate site at Vaucluse, the 1911 press headlines of a 'Japanese scare', the artillery guards quietly posted at the South Head forts although no evidence of spying was found, and how Edgeworth David's attention and friendship turned public perception, with visits by children and the Vaucluse Council won over.

National Diet Library, Japan, 'SHIRASE Nobu', Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures (English and Japanese pages read, short biography), with the NDL Digital Collections item record of 'Akita-ken shashin-roku' (pid 1087219) for the portrait. Short biography: explorer born in Akita, military officer moved early to the reserve, joined Gunji Shigetada's 1893 Kuril expedition and wintered on Shimushu, changed his target from the North Pole to the South Pole after the American claim, obtained the support of Okuma Shigenobu and the newspaper and magazine companies, left Shinagawa in November 1910 on the Kainan Maru with 26 crew, landed in January 1912 and reached 80 degrees 05 minutes S, which he named Yamato Snow Plain.

persistence.rationale: [src_shirase_barr, src_shirase_newscientist, src_shirase_summerson, src_shirase_dos, src_shirase_ausmuseum | 1893-1935 | scholarly report, science journalism, academic chapter, city reference history, museum history] Barr records that at Shimushu he stayed a second winter after ten of the party had died; after the 1911 season failed too late in the year he wintered at Sydney, sent men home for funds and dogs, and sailed again on 19 November 1911 (Barr, Summerson, New Scientist, Dictionary of Sydney); and Barr says it took him until 1935 and many lectures to pay back the expedition debt. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 78 / 0.68 because the second Kuril winter and the debt repayment rest on one report that draws on the expedition's own records and the museum's paper, while the second voyage depended heavily on Okuma and David. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (Roster67 lead review): 74@0.64 -> 72@0.58. Barr, Summerson and the news piece all lean on the 1913 expedition report; independent confirmation of the later years is thin.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_shirase_newscientist, src_shirase_barr, src_shirase_summerson, src_shirase_ndl | 1893-1911 | science journalism, scholarly report, academic chapter, national library biography] With no tradition of polar exploration in Japan he put a budget to the Diet in January 1910, and when the government would not pay the sum voted he set up a private supporters' association and raised the money from donors and Okuma (Barr, New Scientist, NDL); during the Sydney winter he sent his secretary and the captain home to raise funds and bring dogs (Barr, Summerson). The founding acts are documented by three sources, but they all follow the expedition's own account and the same Okuma-led story. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.64 because the funding story is told almost entirely from the expedition's own account and Okuma's rescue was decisive. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (Roster67 lead review): 72@0.6 -> 70@0.55. fundraising/planning narrative is retold across sources of one lineage.

adaptability.rationale: [src_shirase_barr, src_shirase_newscientist, src_shirase_ndl, src_shirase_summerson | 1909-1912 | scholarly report, science journalism, national library biography, academic chapter] After Peary and Cook's claims in 1909 he turned from a North Pole expedition to the South Pole (NDL, Barr); in Sydney in 1911 the expedition gave up the Pole and planned exploration in two parties instead, and in January 1912 he again changed the plan on the ice by putting the Dash Patrol ashore at a different spot and splitting the party (Barr, New Scientist, Summerson). Three or more distinct changes of aim are documented by independent accounts. Reviewed in self-calibration and kept. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (Roster67 lead review): 72@0.62 -> 70@0.56. the 1909 strategy change is told from one expedition-report lineage; strong_inference at 0.62 overstated the independent support.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_shirase_newscientist, src_shirase_barr, src_shirase_summerson | 1893-1912 | science journalism, scholarly report, academic chapter] He took a 204-ton converted fisheries ship into Antarctic waters after a late start, which the New Zealand press judged ill-prepared (New Scientist, Barr), joined the Kuril winters that killed many of the party (Barr), and left for the Dash Patrol with provisions for 20 days; he also halted the patrol when the food ran short and the expedition ended the voyage at a conference on 14 February (Barr, Summerson), so the exposure was accepted but bounded. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.56 because the sources disagree on how reckless the first season was (late funding delayed the sailing) and the Dash Patrol was halted cautiously.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_shirase_barr, src_shirase_ausmuseum, src_shirase_dos, src_shirase_summerson | 1910-1912 | scholarly report, museum history, city reference history, academic chapter] With little money he bought a small fisheries ship, recruited two Ainu dog drivers when ponies would not fit (Barr), and in Sydney obtained a site on the Wentworth estate, David's practical help and a landing exemption for the scientists (Dictionary of Sydney, Australian Museum). Dogs were tested for tapeworm before the second voyage after the first season's losses (Barr). SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.58 because most of the practical improvisation is in one report, much of the Sydney help came from David and the landowner, and the first season's dog losses cut the other way.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_shirase_barr, src_shirase_newscientist, src_shirase_ausmuseum | 1910-1911 | scholarly report, science journalism, museum history] Barr says the Diet voted funds after he argued that the expedition would help Japan become a rich and powerful nation, and he won Okuma's backing and small student donations, while Edgeworth David took up his cause in Sydney (Barr, New Scientist, Australian Museum). The government did not pay, the press mocked the idea, and it was Okuma and David who turned the outcome. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.50, strong_inference, because the record shows others carried the persuading and his own arguments are known only from the expedition account.

discipline.rationale: [src_shirase_newscientist, src_shirase_barr | 1880s-1935 | science journalism, scholarly report] New Scientist says that to harden himself he gave up drink and tobacco, kept away from the fire in winter and refused hot food and drink, and Barr records that he repaid the expedition debt over about two decades while living in relative poverty. The regimen is reported by one article and the debt repayment is a persistence fact, so the claim is modest. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.44 because the regimen rests on one article and the later repayment says more about persistence than routine.

portrait.source: Photograph of Shirase Nobu in army uniform with medals (photographer not named), printed in an oval on a plate of sixteen portraits with the printed caption 南極探険隊長たりし陸軍中尉 白瀬矗君 (Army Lieutenant Shirase Nobu, leader of the Antarctic expedition) and his Tokyo address, in the picture book Akita-ken shashin-roku (compiled by the Akita Photograph Exchange Society, Tsuchizaki-minato, Taisho 6 = 1917), digitised in the National Diet Library Digital Collections (item 1087219, page 23) and shown on the library's site Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures. The image is the site's 421 x 821 pixel file, used as is: not resized and not upscaled.
portrait.license: Public domain: photograph published in Japan in 1917 (before 1958, so its Japanese copyright had expired and was not restored in the United States); the National Diet Library item record carries the Public Domain Mark (rights code pdm, permission rule internet), and the library states that all images in the exhibition are in the public domain and may be reused including commercially
portrait.attribution: Photographer unknown; plate in Akita-ken shashin-roku (Akita Photograph Exchange Society, 1917); National Diet Library, Japan, Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures
portrait.creator: Unknown photographer; reproduced in Akita-ken shashin-roku (Akita Photograph Exchange Society)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (lead) / REPLACED. The lead, Commons 'Nobu Shirase.jpg', cites only the 1956-or-earlier Japanese book 'Meiji no yume kobo' (Ushio Shuppansha) with 'before 1956' as its date and no photographer or first-publication evidence, so its public-domain basis was not verified and it was not used. REPLACEMENT: the National Diet Library Portraits photograph, which the library's own data (read from its site database) draws from page 23 of Akita-ken shashin-roku, compiled by the Akita Photograph Exchange Society, Taisho 6 (1917). NDL item record (API, pid 1087219): permission rule 'internet', rights code 'pdm' (Public Domain Mark), not 'undetermined'; the NDL 'About This Site' page states all images in the exhibition are public domain and reusable without application, including for commercial use. I opened the whole page scan through IIIF: it is a plate of sixteen oval portraits and the lower-left oval is captioned 南極探険隊長たりし陸軍中尉 白瀬矗君 plus a Tokyo address in Naka-Shibuya-cho, so identity does not rest on the NDL page alone. The NDL site file (421 x 821) is crisper than a native crop of the IIIF scan (about 346 x 653), so it is used as is, with no resizing. Photographer unknown and the sitting date unknown (before 1917, after his 1912 return judging by the medals and rank). Legal basis does not depend on the photographer: published in Japan in 1917. KIND likeness. PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-13, Wikidata API) Q715832 label 'Nobu Shirase', description 'Japanese explorer of the Antarctic (1861-1946)', ja 白瀬矗, ko 시라세 노부, born 1861-07-20, died 1946-09-04, human, citizen of Japan; no collision with an existing candidate file, slug or QID. BIRTH DATE: Wikipedia and the Barr paper say 13 June 1861, Wikidata and the NDL say 20 July 1861 (the same day in the lunar and western calendars); only the year 1861 is used. REGION east_asia (Japanese precedent Kuroda Seiki). ERA 20th_century (his expedition was 1910-12; precedent Kuroda Seiki). NATIONALITY JP. ZERO POLITICS / MILITARY: primary identity is polar explorer. His army reserve commission and service in the Sino-Japanese and Russo-Japanese wars, the Kuril colonisation purpose of the Gunji expedition, the covert-mission claims in some sources and his claiming of Yamato Snow Plain for Japan are context only and unscored. VOCABULARY: occupation explorer; field exploration; impact domain historical (the New Scientist historians judge the scientific results minimal, so no scientific domain); tags explorer, leader; archetype organizational_leader (precedent Robert Falcon Scott); all labelled in EN and KO. KO NAME 시라세 노부 is the Wikidata label. ATTRIBUTION: attributable (dated expedition with a published official report, press coverage in New Zealand and Australia, and the diaries of the Fram crew). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Susan Barr, 'The Japanese Antarctic Expedition in 1912', Nankyoku Shiryo 57(2), 2013. READ (6 sources besides Wikidata and Wikipedia): Barr (full, archived PDF); Pain in New Scientist (full, via a blog mirror); Summerson in ANU Press (full chapter); Australian Museum sword page and blog (full); Dictionary of Sydney (full); NDL biography. Also read and not cited: Wired for Adventure and Antarctica21 popular summaries (they contain errors such as a 1883 Kuril posting), Quark and Antarctic Logistics summaries, the front matter of McInnes's 2009 thesis (only abstract and contents were available). NOT OPENED: Hamre 1933 (JSTOR), the 2011 translation of the expedition report, Shirase's own Nankyoku tanken, Chet Ross's bibliography, the McInnes and Stevenson theses beyond their front matter, Trove newspaper articles. PERSPECTIVES: (1) polar historian's report (Barr); (2) science journalism citing two academic historians and the NZ/Australian press (Pain); (3) an academic chapter surveying the English and Japanese literature (Summerson); (4) Australian local institutions and the 1911 Sydney press (Australian Museum, Dictionary of Sydney); (5) national library biography. NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL SOURCES: all of the above; but Barr, Summerson and Pain rely on the 1913 expedition report written by Shirase's supporters' association for the events on the ice, so the behavioural evidence is thin in independence for the Antarctic days. CONTRADICTIONS AND LIMITS: Dash Patrol distance is 237, 250 or about 280 km depending on the source; the departure date from Tokyo is 29 November (Barr) or 1 December (Summerson, Antarctica21); the Australian Museum blog's Alaska claim conflicts with the Kuril account; the Kainan Maru's easternmost point is 152 W (Summerson) or 155 W (Antarctic Logistics). Barr's account of the Dash Patrol says the Fram's Norwegian crew found the Japanese ship dirty and their handling of seals and penguins cruel, which is a counter-voice from the Fram diaries and is not scored. Scientific results were minimal (New Scientist). No adversarial biography exists in English; the closest counter-voice is the Fram diaries as quoted by Barr and the New Scientist historians. CONCENTRATION: 4 rows lowered for source-family concentration (persistence, resourcefulness, persuasiveness, discipline); proactive_agency and risk_tolerance lowered in self-calibration on other grounds; adaptability kept. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE: cards (1) leading the Japanese Antarctic Expedition 1910-12 with the Dash Patrol to 80 degrees 05 minutes S, (2) recognition and the Shirase name in the Antarctic and the icebreakers. Debt repayment is a moment, not a card. Match eligibility is not assessed here (7 rows). shirase-nobu:persistence RUBRIC_CORRECTION (Roster67 lead review): 74@0.64 -> 72@0.58.
